newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin wants border patrols with neutral Finns.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin wants border patrols with neutral Finns.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin said on Saturday Finland and Russia should mount joint patrols along their long border to save money and underscore close ties between a non-NATO Western state and the Kremlin.

He told reporters before Finnish President Martti Ahtisaari arrived for two days of informal talks at his holiday retreat that he would also propose opening up 13 islands in the Gulf of Finland that have been off-limits to Finns for 40 years.

"How much money do we waste on border activities? And how much do they waste, too?" Yeltsin said in his remarks at his woodland residence in Karelia, a northwest Russian region that was once part of Finland.
"Look, we are two presidents, let's get together. Let's look after the border jointly -- it will be half the price."
Russia is battling to reform and cut the size of its armed forces to make them more efficient and to reduce the country's budget deficit.
Moscow is also keen to minimise the effect of NATO's planned eastward expansion. The defence alliance this week invited the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland to join.

It was not clear whether Ahtisaari would back the proposal to mount joint patrols along the 1270-km (790-mile) border. Finland is neutral but has pledged to work closely with NATO. It has no immediate plans to try to join the alliance.

Yeltsin, who did not explicitly link his proposal to NATO expansion, said the idea came to him since he started his holiday in Karelia last weekend. He said the border was between two close neighbours rather than a faultline between blocs.
"It is not as if we border a military power," Yeltsin was quoted as saying by Itar-Tass news agency.
Finland has 3,500 frontier guards. Russia's border guards number 100,000 -- stretched out along its enormous frontiers with a dozen countries across as many time zones.
Yeltsin also took a gentle swipe at NATO expansion plans, pointedly saying he much preferred the temperature in Karelia to the climes of Madrid, where the alliance held its summit.

He told reporters he was prepared to open access to islands declared closed to Finns in 1956. He said he would propose jointly developing at least one or two of the islands as tourist centres and splitting the profits with Finland.
He said he was enjoying his holiday in the deep forests of Karelia. He was swimming every day in the lake near his residence and taking a Russian "banya" steam bath to warm up.
He said that on Friday he played tennis, his favourite sport, for the first time since heart surgery last November.
"I'm not up to competing yet," he said. "But it is a start."
